MR. RYNARD-ADEQUACY OF ANSWER TO ORDER PAPER QUESTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege in respect of question No. 1,443, the answer to which appears at page 5768 of Hansard for April 13. On March 5 I placed this question on the Order Paper:
1.	How many companies, building plants in designated areas, are controlled outside of Canada?
2.	How many are Canadian companies?
3.	What was the cost in dollars for machinery and equipment purchased outside of Canada by companies controlled outside of Canada?
4.	What was the cost in dollars of machinery and equipment purchased in Canada by foreign subsidiaries?
5.	What percentage of machinery and equipment was obtainable in Canada at competitive prices?
The purpose of the first part of the question was to elicit information concerning the number of foreign-controlled subsidiaries qualifying for assistance in designated areas. This is a question of extreme importance to the Canadian people who are supplying the money to these designated areas.
Next I wanted to know the number of Canadian companies so that we would have a comparison between foreign-owned subsidiaries and Canadian-owned companies qualifying for assistance. The third part of the question concerned how much machinery and equipment for these industries was purchased outside Canada which could have been purchased in this country at a competitive price from Canadian factories employing Canadian workers.
I would have thought the government would be pleased to furnish this information to the Canadian people. The curt answer given on April 13 in effect was that the information is denied because no Act of Parliament makes the government give this information, and it is then stated in the answer that the information is not available. I believe this published answer to be false.

Why is this information hidden from the Canadian people? As the humble servant of my riding I ask that this information be made available to the Canadian people.

1.	Has CBC presented an account for expenses incurred during the fiscal year 1968-69 through the reservation of hotel rooms not subsequently used and, if so, what was the total of such expenses?
2.	Will the government require the employees of the corporation to provide receipts and statements?

I am informed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as follows: As a matter of policy CBC employees are required to account to the Corporation for expenses incurred on CBC business. Normally the responsibility to cancel hotel reservations not actually required rests with the employees concerned. However, under extraordinary circumstances and upon satisfactory evidence and explanation, expense incurred by not using reservations may be borne by the Corporation. Prior to coverage of the U.S. political conventions in 1968 it was necessary to make reservations and advance deposits for hotel accommodation through the Republican and Democratic housing committees in order to ensure availability of hotel accommodation for both CBC English and French network production personnel covering these conventions. In the case of the Republican convention, reservations had to be made before exact requirements were determined and $100 was forfeited when two of the rooms booked were not needed. At the time of the Democratic convention in Chicago, the accommodation reserved for the CBC was left unused due to the development of riots, which altered CBC coverage plans and led to arrangements for alternative accommodation, notably a move to other quarters in the interest of safety for CBC personnel who had originally been assigned a hotel in the midst of the riot area. A total of $700. was therefore forfeited in connection with the Chicago convention coverage.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for Exter-
Inquiries of the Ministry nal Affairs regarding the transportation of a large quantity of nerve gas from Okinawa to Bangor, Washington, passing through the Strait of Juan de Fuca. In view of the growing concern in the United States and Canada regarding the hazard which might follow any mishap, I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs if he can tell the House whether there has been communicated to him the date on which this shipment will take place, what precautions are being taken, and if the minister is satisfied with those precautions as they affect the lives of Canadian citizens?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRANSFER OF NERVE GAS FROM OKINAWA TO UNITED STATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in answer to the first question, I do not think that the United States government has yet made a decision on the date of shipment. As to the second question, we have received from the United States government, in response to our request for information and our expressions of concern, information about the precautions being taken. This information is being studied by the government. We are also expressing to the United States government, more formally than in the past and on the basis of the information received, the grave concern we have about the possibility of an accident.

subtopic: TRANSFER OF NERVE GAS FROM OKINAWA TO UNITED STATES
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. May I ask the minister if he intends to ascertain the date when the shipment will take place and if he intends to have his study completed in sufficient time so that the government of Canada can express to the government of the United States any concern it may have about the inadequacy of the precautions which are being taken?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRANSFER OF NERVE GAS FROM OKINAWA TO UNITED STATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is my understanding that the United States government has not yet made a decision as to when the shipments will begin. On the second point, we are of course concerned notwithstanding the kinds of precautions that are being taken. We understand these are very thorough and very extensive. But there always remains the possibility of an accident, and therefore it would not matter what information we received about these precautions; we would still have reason for the concern that I have expressed to the United States government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enter this debate in order to deal with the problems that have arisen as a result of the mismanagement by the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans), and later by the government, of the postal situation in Montreal. I do that because Your Honour yesterday held you could not allow a motion under Standing Order 26 and suggested that one of the reasons was the opportunity that the budget debate would give us to deal with this matter.
I hope Your Honour will not think me presumptuous if I take advantage of this opportunity to suggest very respectfully that an omnibus budget debate is really not a substitute for a debate on a special matter of specific importance. I took the occasion this morning to notify the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) and the Minister of Communications that I intended to seek the floor this afternoon, and I indicated the purpose for which I would seek it.
I notice that the President of the Treasury Board at least is in the chamber. If he intends to sit through my remarks, I wish to express to him my appreciation. But I do hold, as I said, with the greatest respect, that whatever the situation in the past may have been, under the new rules an omnibus debate such as the Throne Speech debate or the Budget debate does not really meet the situation usually sought by a member for a special debate to deal with a special emergency for which he considers it important to have a debate in the House.
There may have been other reasons for Your Honour not allowing the motion, but I thought that with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would make the comment that it is a small consolation to be able to make a speech in an ominbus debate instead of having the attention of all hon. members directed to one point which a motion under Standing Order 26 would do.

speechtext:
At the outset I want to make clear that my colleagues and I regret very much the violence which has taken place in Montreal as a result of the difficulties that have arisen. Not only do we not condone that violence, but I take the liberty to express the hope on behalf of my colleagues and myself- and I am sure on behalf of every member of this House-that the violence will end, that whoever may be responsible for it will avoid escalating it so that some solution may be found in an atmosphere other than one of violence.
There has been talk, particularly by the Minister of Communications, about not yielding to blackmail. I say to him that as one who has had some experience in labour relations I am thoroughly fed up with an employer talking about blackmail when his employees are making certain demands. I say to the minister and to the government that if the word "blackmail" is applicable in this situation at all, it is applicable to the occupants of the treasury benches who are saying to the employees involved, "Either you sign up by midnight, Wednesday, April 15, or you are without a job". If that is not blackmail, I would like to know what is. But in any case, using the word "blackmail" does not help us very much one way or the other.
It may well be that the wrong road along which the government has travelled on this issue has brought it into a corner so that it now has no alternative but to stick by its present position. It may well be that the situation in Montreal is now so complicated and so perverse that it is impossible for the government to reverse its position and take another line. I hope not. I hope the government can still see its way clear to do what in my submission should have been done in the first place.
But if it is in that corner and if, as a result, there should be greater disruption and continuing violence in Montreal which, as I have said, I hope with all my heart will not be the case, I say that the responsibility will be entirely that of the government and of every member of this government, particularly those members whose labour history many of us respect very deeply, as I do. I refer in
April 15, 1970

particular to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand). That a government which has him as a member, as well as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mack-asey) and the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier), who was once on the staff of the CNTU in Quebec, should have so utterly, completely and callously mismanaged the situation in Montreal I suggest to you, Sir, speaks volumes for the fact that when this government comes to deal with ordinary people, with working people, with labouring people, it does not deserve to govern. There is no other conclusion possible.
I think that what has happened in this case has been a complete negation of some very basic principles to which this government should have been committed. I will try to suggest to Your Honour and to the government that what has happened in this case is a complete negation of the spirit of the Freedman report which the Minister of Labour has said he intends to legislate upon as soon as he produces his intended amendments to the relevant statute.
What did the Freedman report say in effect, without referring to the actual words? What Mr. Justice Freedman said was, in moral and social terms-and the President of the Treasury Board had better not smile because I suggest to him that this is accurate-

I assume that is what he was rising to say, Mr. Speaker. What Mr. Justice Freedman said, and what every modern thinker on labour relations and industrial democracy in every western country has said, is that in the modern society it should not be free to an employer, or indeed to a group of employers, to make changes in their operations, to introduce efficiencies in their operations at the expense of the employees without consulting the union concerned before the decision to change the operations is made, and without working out some program 22218-27$
The Budget-Mr. Lewis which will at least reduce the hardship imposed on the employees as a result of that change. I will indicate, I think factually, that the government-perhaps not all of the government was involved in the early stages-or at least the Postmaster General and Minister of Communications violated that principle.
Aside from what Mr. Justice Freedman has said, it seems to me clear that the government of Canada, and the government of any democratic country, ought to be a model employer. It ought to act in such a way that every citizen in the country can see the concern which government has and which society collectively has and should have for the rights and the welfare of ordinary working people, and the rights of the union that represents them.
Thirdly, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the action of the minister and of the government in this case has been another denial of all the protestations about participatory democracy, in any meaningful sense of that term. What happened in this case? The Post Office authorities, perhaps for good reason-I do not know-decided that the arrangement which they had had in the past and which was to end on March 31 of this year was inefficient and that they wanted to change it. So they called for tenders from contractors to do the job of picking up and delivering the mail.
What was the first duty of the government, Mr. Speaker, if it was a government with any principle whatsoever relating to decent labour relations, if it was a government acting in a way in which everyone in this House and everyone in Canada has the right to expect it to act? What should have been the first thing the Postmaster General should have done in his invitation for tenders? I suggest that the invitation ought to have contained, as a condition of the tender, a guarantee of the job security of the employees, a guarantee of their wage schedule and a guarantee of the continuation of their bargaining rights. I have looked at the documents that were filed, and I can say that the failure to have any one of those conditions in the invitation to tender was a callous disruption of the lives and the security of some 450 workers and their families. In a moment I will indicate why, in my opinion, that was not done, Mr. Speaker.
So the Postmaster General got five contractors every one of whom, according to my information-four out of the five, at least, according to the documents tabled by the President of the Treasury Board-

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

Well, four contractors; and all were shadow corporations that were not in existence. They did not exist as corporations; they were merely individuals who signed letters of intent with the government, I suppose undertaking to go through the necessary legal steps to incorporate themselves for the purpose for which they were tendering. These shadow corporations, from which the government did not have any bond and from which the government could not obtain any guarantee, were allowed to sign agreements with the government, and the government signed contracts with them, to do this job without any guarantee for the security of the workers, for their seniority, for their wage rights or for their bargaining rights.
Is anyone in this House or in the country surprised that when that was done the workers resented it, and that they would take whatever steps, in their desperation, they thought were open to them at that time.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Condoning violence?

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Not including violence, Mr. Speaker. I have said already that I regret the violence. But I say to the President of the Treasury Board that it is easier for him and for me to advise that people contain themselves and control themselves than it is for people who are hurt to do so. It is the fault of those who provoke the situation that creates the violence, just as much as it is the fault of those who engage in the violence. I am not condoning the violence, but I say that the Postmaster General, his department and his associates in the government who acted so meanly as well as so stupidly provoked a situation which they should have known would lead to violence, and it is their responsibility just as much as it is the responsibility of those in Montreal who have engaged in violence.
It is possible for the people in Montreal to stop their violence, as I appeal to them to do, but it is apparently not possible for the people in Montreal to get the government to reverse its stupid and mean actions of the past. Now the workers are in the position that either they accept the conditions the government is forcing on them or they remain unemployed, with their families in the condition in which the families of unemployed people usually find themselves. It is the government's fault, Mr. Speaker, and not the fault of the people concerned.

Having heard about this, having had the pleasure and the honour of being visited by a committee of the union in early March-I did not bother looking up the date-when they told me about the situation in Montreal-

The Minister of Communications ought to have the humility not to make that kind of remark, in view of the mess for which he is responsible. If there is a minister of this or any other government who has been responsible for as many messes in labour relations in a department as he has been in the Post Office, I think that government ought to look at itself very seriously.
When I had the pleasure of being visited by a committee of the union-the minister has reminded me of when it was, and in a moment I will tell the House why he knows the date-some time in February and I listened to their story of this situation, I immediately remembered and drew to their attention a section of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, under which the union of course had been certified by the Canada Labour Relations Board.
I immediately drew their attention to section 9 (3) of that act which permits a bargaining unit for more than one employer if all the employers concerned consent thereto. I said to the union that it seemed to me that was their answer, that they should persuade the government to make a condition of the contracts with these contractors that they should all consent to one bargaining unit for all their employees collectively, under section 9 (3) of the act, and if necessary they should go to the Canada Labour Relations Board for confirmation of that. Then their bargaining rights, their bargaining unit and the bargaining agent would continue as previously and there would be no disruption of their situation.
The members of the union committee who were in my office at the time said, "Mr. Lewis, the government won't do that." I asked them, "Why do you say no?" They replied "Because the present contractors cannot meet
April 15, 1970

the requirements of our present collective agreement, and therefore the government will not be able to twist the arms of the contractors to agree to one bargaining unit as provided in the law."

Realizing the seriousness of the situation in Montreal, I took it upon myself to visit the Minister of Communications the day following or within a day or two of having met this committee. He was good enough to express to me some of the problems he had in the situation. Obviously, they were very real and very serious problems: I do not deny that. I drew his attentiotn to the same section of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act and urged him to take steps to get the contractors to agree to have the one bargaining unit continue as the bargaining agent. In this way, he could have both objectives. Instead of having one contractor doing the job from one headquarters in Montreal, he could have had his four contractors, with the resulting economies which he hoped to achieve by dividing Montreal into four regions. At the same time the workers would have had their seniority, job security, wages and so on guaranteed.
He had not known about that section in the act. I do not blame him for that because it was not his field, as it had been mine for some years. He told me that he would immediately see the Minister of Labour and the Deputy Minister and discuss it with them. Some days later when I asked in this Chamber what had happened, the minister replied that he could not do that because one of the employers was connected with the Teamsters Union. I do not have the answer before me, but that is my clear memory of it.
I have investigated that statement, Mr. Speaker. I regret that it was given by a responsible and respected person-because I do respect him. His reply to my question was the kind of half-truth which demolishes the integrity of the person giving it. I did not speak to the employer concerned, but I am informed that it is true that one employer had some connection with the Teamsters Union. However, the separate unit that was to be created for carrying out the operations under the Post Office contract had nothing to do with the union.

He was one party to the contract with these people and he could have said to them, "As a condition of the contract you have to agree to the employees being in one bargaining unit." That would have made good sense, aside from the difficulties in Montreal.
No employer who wants industrial peace, no employer who is not interested in disrupting labour relations would be happy with a situation where you had four contractors, all doing the same work, the employees of each contractor doing the same work, four separate bargaining units and four separate contracts. No employer in his right mind wants that. Perhaps that is the answer-that the right mind was not there.
When it was suggested to the minister that he get these contractors to agree to one bargaining unit, the suggestion was not merely a concession to the workers. It was a good suggestion in itself from the point of view of labour relations. It was much better to have one contract and one bargaining unit for employees of all contractors doing the same work than four competing contracts with four competing unions trying to outnegotiate each other. There was an easy, simple, human solution, but the Postmaster General would have none of it. Why? Because he did not want the CNTU to remain.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
One of the reasons why I say this, Mr. Speaker-I do it with some hesitation, but I think the situation is so serious that it ought to be made public-is that I am informed on the best authority that there is in the hands of Mr. Goldenberg, the commissioner, a memorandum made at his request in which the Minister of Communications and/or one or other of his officers is quoted as saying that one of the purposes of the entire exercise was to get rid of this CNTU local in the situation in Montreal.
The existence of that memorandum about which I was assured and from which the person who spoke to me had made notes at one point-how he obtained it, I do not know-made me ask the other day that all the documents in Mr. Goldenberg's possession be tabled. When the minister yesterday tabled the documents other than those that were confidential, I shouted across the floor, perhaps improperly, Mr. Speaker, that of course the interesting documents would not be there. Of course they were not, because I suppose that was a confidential document.
That is the first point I make, Mr. Speaker; that the employees and the union concerned were convinced that one of the purposes of the exercise of four contracts of a certain type in a certain context was to get rid of the union. The suspicion was confirmed by what was seen in a memorandum in the confidential possession of Mr. Carl Goldenberg. In Mr. Goldenberg's report there is a clear statement of the reason why the Postmaster General did not want to do what was obviously the right thing, namely, get one bargaining unit and the same bargaining agent. At line 7, page 7, of Mr. Goldenberg's report he deals with the various contracts with the employers as follows:
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I am not in a position to pass a proper judgement on their bids but, on the basis of contemplated wage rates and the attitude to labour relations disclosed to me, I am of the opinion that they-
Namely, the contractors.
-will be unable to fulfil their commitments within the fixed price and, at the same time, maintain industrial peace.
In plain English, as I read Mr. Goldenberg's words, he is saying that the Postmaster General signed the kind of contract with the contractors which made it impossible for them to pay wage rates to the truck drivers which the truck drivers were then receiving, that the contractors had indicated they were not interested in decent labour relations and that therefore the whole thing could not work. That is why nothing was done about using the instrument of the federal labour law in settling the problem in such a way that the employers and the union concerned would have no difficulty.

speechtext:
Sir, I did not realize the time had slipped by so quickly. That was the way, in my submission, to have solved the problem and guaranteed the people the rights they were entitled to. As Mr. Goldenberg points out in that report, we are not dealing with novices, with men who had just started work in this field. We are dealing with men with very considerable service. Mr. Goldenberg sets this out right at the opening of his report, at the bottom of page 2. Of these employees 20 of the 450 had a seniority of 20 years or more, and 88 had a seniority of between 10 and 20 years. So a total of 108 had a seniority of more than 10 years. Of the other employees, 85 had a seniority of between 5 and 10 years. Therefore, a total of almost 200 had a seniority of more than 5 years, and 159 had a seniority of between 2 and 5 years. Of the 450 employees, 360 or so had a seniority of more than two years and about half of that total had seniority of more than ten years. That is a considerable length of service.
In our modern society a man does not work for wages alone. He does not merely acquire wages. In a good union and labour relations situation he also acquires an equity in his job resulting from seniority and other benefits he is able to win collectively through his trade union. By ignoring this, the government caused desperation among these men for no reason whatsoever. That is what made the men so angry about the situation. There was no reason for its happening.
The Postmaster General had it within his power early in February to act wisely. Indeed if he had taken advice, as he should have months before that he would have been able to settle the problem in such a way that the CNTU local would remain and the CNTU bargaining agent would remain, the people concerned would have been reassured about their wages and job security. All this could have been done months ago by the simple application of section 9(3) of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act.
Even though he did not do this before February, and even though his attention was drawn to this matter-it so happens I was the one who drew it to his attention-six or seven weeks before the deadline would have been time enough for him to carry out the policy that would have avoided the desperation, the violence and the disruption that has taken place and threatens to continue in
The Budget-Mr. Lewis Montreal. We are in this mess because of the complete insensitivity of the Postmaster General to the rights of workers.
I am reminded-if I may interrupt myself for a moment-that even a good person cannot escape his background. No one denies that the Postmaster General is a well-meaning person. But his having been president of the Canadian Stock Exchange and the Montreal Stock Exchange was simply not the kind of training that makes possible a good appreciation of labour relations involving ordinary working people in a situation as critical as the one in Montreal. He ought to have stood aside and allowed someone who displayed some sensitivity to labour relations to take over.
The government, having brought the country and the people of Montreal to this mess, then appointed Mr. Goldenberg as a commissioner. He recommended that the government take over the operation in Montreal. It so happens that I have had the pleasure of knowing Mr. Goldenberg since my undergraduate days at McGill ever so many years ago; I hate to say how many. I think Mr. Goldenberg was wrong. I think the advice he gave the government was wrong. It would have made sense if his advice had been that all people who do similar work across Canada everywhere, in every centre of the country, be public servants and in the public service. If that had been the advice and if the government had applied it throughout the country, that would have been one way of acting. But when you enforce on the drivers in Montreal a decision based upon a report designed to clean up a mess for which the government was responsible, that is another thing. The advice was not well based and the government was not wise in accepting it.
I shall not take much more time. I am grateful to hon. members for allowing me this additional time. I wanted to put these things on record for three reasons. First, this is an example of the attitude of this government towards labour relations, and it frightens the hell out of me. It frightens me beyond words that a relatively uncomplicated situation which ought to have been relatively easy to control should have been permitted to develop the way it has developed, with all the consequences it will have on the lives of about 459 Canadians and their families in Montreal. That frightens me and indicates an attitude toward labour relations by the government that does not bode well for the future of that aspect of Canada's activities.

April 15, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Lewis
Second, one can be disturbed also by the way in which this government has dealt with labour relations in the total Public Service. Postal unions are now undergoing a process of conciliation after six months of negotiation. This is the kind of thing that creates bitterness. Third, one hopes that there is still time for the government to change its attitude and to revert to original policy and try to find a responsible contractor or two, three or four contractors in Montreal. I am sure there are such contractors who would take on this job on tenders which would enable them to pay decent wages to the truck drivers, wages similar to those the truck drivers have received until now. In that context the truck drivers ought to be allowed to continue their union membership and their union and collective bargaining rights. There is still time for the government to do this.
I appeal to the two ministers here to take another look at the situation and see whether they cannot do some of the simple things I have suggested, for I fear if the government does not, if the government remains adamant, two things will-not may-happen. One will be a continuing disruption of the postal service in Canada's largest city, accompanied possibly with continued strife and violence. Although I hope there will not be violence, I know enough about the situation to realize that there well may be violence. The second thing that will happen is that several hundred Canadians will be without a job and on the unemployment rolls which this government's policy has increased in size, particularly in Quebec and in Montreal.

I have been convinced for weeks that the government's case was far from strong. The exchanges we have heard this afternoon, on the lines of "you did-I didn't" convince me that its case is indeed abysmally weak.
I am sure no man of the stature of the hon. member for York South would in any way rejoice at violence. Nor would I. But the fact is, things have happened in Montreal in recent weeks and this, together with recent fiascos in the management field, would lead anyone interested in the social scene to fear a recurrence. I am one of those who believe in vigorous protest but never in violent protest. Never at any time have I had conversations with the men involved here, or with the union. I am prepared, however, to accept the charge of being emotional. I am definitely susceptible to emotion on occasions where human suffering is involved. If I say I am profoundly disturbed by the thought of what it may mean to their dependants, let me point out that after many agonizing weeks of uncertainty, of brittleness and expectance of

I think, too, that this long and agonizing problem affects more than the unions and more than cabinet members in their relevant positions within cabinet; it affects the public not only in Montreal but in all of Canada. The government, through whichever minister at a given time was its spokesman, has been far less than sufficiently forthcoming in dealing with the problems of these people. Such information we have has been received through press releases or through speculative reports of digging newspapermen. This is not good enough. The people of Canada have a mighty important stake in this matter.
This particular problem is one of the most painful and serious eruptions in the postal service itself. It is an eruption in a service which for a long, long time has been something less than healthy. I am often amazed at the frequent expressions of the daily press that today mail service in Montreal is near normal. Even when it is normal it is terrible. There is a backlog there which is abominable.
I have a file of letters 18 inches high testifying to the outrageous service which is being visited upon the people of Montreal and the people whose service is dependent upon transit of mail through Montreal.
I hope in our great concern for this particular and unique problem we do not forget that the deterioration of the Post Office Department has been a problem for the past few months. As a result of this deplorable mess we have found an incapacity to deal with some basic considerations. There is the question of job security which has been in existence for some time. and that this created a state of fear, insecurity and demoralization. Who would not realize that this would be the kind of reaction of these men, many of whom had been involved in carrying the nation's mail for many years and doing a very good job of it? I notice, as well, that Mr. Goldenberg examined carefully the reasons Lapalme was not able to continue. He goes back to one of the points many of us have been discussing for months and months. He refers to the reduction in postal services from six days to five days. We need not go into that question now, but it will be gone into again and again.
Another interesting thing is that Lapalme advised the union and asked for its co-operation in preparing its tender. Mr. Goldenberg went on to say that considering that tenders would be based on rates of pay below those in effect under the collective agreement, the union refused to negotiate. Accordingly, Lapalme did not tender for any of the five contracts. Much of this problem has stemmed from that will-o-the-wisp search of the Postmaster General for some measure of economy in order that he could somehow, some day in some way prove that, by jove, he would make this department pay. The public will be appalled when the full bill in dollars and cents, to say nothing in terms of human measurements, comes in. This will be one of the most costly fiascos since the costly abandonment of the Prince Edward Island causeway. If the Auditor General is still around next year, I predict he will find an interesting situation here.
I do not know that there is much value in my continuing the denunciation which was so eloquently put forward by the hon. member for York South. We have reached the stage where to condemn is not to be helpful. Surely the government does not need me to dig it deeper into this mess. I would not want to do that at this stage of the game because I think through its ineptitude, at least to the extent of 90 per cent, we are facing a serious situation. I do not know what will be done tomorrow and I do not know where the government will get experienced men. I do not know what is in store for the long-suffering people of Montreal.
I note, to my horror, that in this whole mess there was more concern for the trucks than for the truck drivers, because in one of the contracts with Lapalme there was reference to the fact that the government, if it took over the service, would purchase the trucks. What about the drivers? Perhaps I am
April 15. 1970

being emotional in suggesting that the drivers are more important. We have not been told the story about this cost and I endeavoured yesterday to obtain this information from the minister. He is a little more evasive than the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans) and a little less arrogant, but the combination of the two is not very helpful.
o (4:20 p.m.)

I would say, in the discharge of that duty, there is no room even for self-applause on the part of the President of the Treasury Board. The government has failed abysmally in this matter. I hope in the eleventh hour-

speechtext:
The point I want to make is that we did not suddenly face the employees of Lapalme or the CNTU with a midnight deadline. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) said that we are now exerting this blackmail or pressure on them. This goes back to at least a year ago January. I am sure the hon. member must know this because we went through 32 days of violence and intimidation in February and March of last year. At that time, on March 3, I publicly announced that as a solution I intended to take over the delivery service in Montreal. The terms were almost as generous as those offered by my colleague during the recent negotiations. But the refusal was for exactly the same reason: the refusal was that there was no legal way in which the government could recognize a union prior to taking in its members.
At that time I said that since the members of this particular union had lost their employer, Hod Service Limited, we were now going to substitute ourselves. I said that the great majority of the drivers employed by Rod Service at that time would be offered employment, and I urged them to report for work as usual on March 14. The following day the postmaster of Montreal sent out a letter. Within 24 hours of the members acting on their own accord we had well over 200 applications. But that particular arrangement was not consummated or completed because the union began to think of itself and its position rather than that of its members. So eventually, since the union had had a collective agreement with an employer, Rod Service, that was to last until March 31, 1970, we in the Post Office decided we would recognize that agreement although it was not our responsibility that they had lost their employer. Their employer, working with them, could ho longer provide the services to which the people of Montreal were entitled.
We decided to ask other people and to approach many trucking firms in Montreal to See whether they were interested in taking

over the contracts and the members. We were successful in doing so. At that time over a year ago-this is not midnight tonight-we warned the members of the union that this was the last one-year contract. We advised them that whatever might be the solution, whether the government would take over the services or go to tender as it does throughout the country, there would be a different solution to the problem because, as my colleague has said, this insecurity and uncertainty has recurred annually.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
It was not good for them, it was not good for the Post Office and it certainly was not good for the people of Montreal because in the three years up to that time there had been five stoppages of work and five threats which have been carried out, of which only one was legal. They were clearly warned. They were also told at the same time that instead of 398 employees, the Post Office felt that the work could be done by a reallocation of the work load, by a scrapping of the old method of dividing services provided into departments and rearranging them geographically into sectors. We believed that this would lead to increasing productivity and would lower the cost to the taxpayers of Canada. In effect, while we agreed to Lapalme taking over 396 employees, we felt that progressively the work could be done by fewer and fewer people and that the appropriate number, including management personnel and supervisory staff, might be something like 330.
They were well aware of this, but during the past year the members acquired control of the union and of the 459 members only three, the two Lapalme brothers who own the operation and their general manager, Mr. Breton, were not members of the union. They progressively increased the cost to the people of Canada. So that the staff did not go down from 396 to 330 but went up from 396 to 459.
I do not wish to recite all of the attendant malpractices both from a union point of view as well as a management point of view that have taken place during the past year, because I do not wish to criticize either union or management here. Suffice it to say that there was every justification for looking for better ways of providing service to the people of Montreal, and the Post Office was bound in its responsibility to the taxpayers of Canada to seek them. This we did.
April 15, 1970

It is not midnight to night that becomes a sudden threat, as the hon. member for York South seeks to imply. But even leaving aside the dates of January, 1969, and March 1969, it was last September when the contractor and the union were officially notified that we intended to go to tenders. Here I refer to the misrepresentation that the hon. member for York South is seeking to impose on this House that some of us on this side have never read the Freedman report or have no understanding of what the report is all about. We do. Mr. Justice Freedman could not have asked for anything more than we have done, because the people who are talking about midnight tonight were notified in September of 1969, which is beyond the six months that Mr. Justice Freedman suggested.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Of what were they notified?

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They were notified that we were going for tenders and that there was therefore a possibility that there would be new employers. So there was a clear indication to everyone concerned. But what happened during the six months was not that they either sought to co-operate with their employer or sought to retain the contracts; in fact, their actions were the complete reverse. So much so-and I come to the famous meeting with the hon. member for York South to which I would not have referred, but he has done it first-that again they lost an employer, and just as Rod Services felt they could no longer continue to operate with the costs, with the lack of productivity, with the lack of loyalty to the service, to the employer and to the people of Montreal, they decided not to submit a tender under the existing contractor's name but to submit a tender under another operation that they control, namely H. Lapalme.
One of the clear advantages of this to the Lapalme brothers was that they felt that in dealing with the Teamsters they would be dealing with a more responsible union that would take account of its contractual obligations. In other words, I am as pro-union as any man in this chamber but I am not one of those who is willing to say that at all times, under all conditions and in all places a union is eternally right. A union, just like a business, large or small, can price itself out of a particular market. This appears to be what the present union is doing.
On February 4 the members of the union went to see the hon. member-it was not in early March-and on February 9 he came to
The Budget-Mr. Kierans see me. We went over the suggestion that he proposed. I was looking for solutions and I told him that I would consider it. But I also presented to him a number of hard facts; that the cost of delivering mail in Montreal had gone up about 73 per cent in four years, whereas the cost of delivering mail in Toronto, with a more rapidly increasing volume and operating from the same base within a difference of three or four cents, had gone up 33 per cent, and that in all conscience as custodian of the public interest I had had to ask for tenders.
I am not saying whether or not he agreed with any of this. I am simply saying that he proposed that I look into the possibility of asking the new contractors to recognize the CNTU in some global fashion or in some partial shape-up fashion, and to agree to hire all the employees that they needed from the prevailing seniority list. But I am sure the hon. member is aware of one fundamental condition in that possibility, that is that the contractors themselves have to agree or consent.
What made his solution impossible is that the contractors would not consent because at this time there was all the evidence of violence which led them, whatever might have been their original intentions, to pull back progressively from hiring those who were responsible for the violence, those who reduced the number of mailboxes in Montreal from 1,800 to 400 and who today fired two bullets into a car in downtown Montreal, a security car protecting the royal mail. They were unwilling, and so the solution that he proposed at that time fell of its own weight. It also fell for another reason, which accounts for the silence of the hon. member since that time, aside from a few inconsequential questions and his last-minute, midnight interest in this problem.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I informed him that one of the contractors to whom we had given the contract was H. Lapalme Transport Ltee., that this man had a union, and that that union was the Teamsters. It is all very well for the hon. member to hint, suggest and imply that legally it would have been possible for him to set up another phantom company, but the contract was not given to another phantom company; it was given to H. Lapalme Transport Ltee., and precisely for the reasons that, according to him at the time, he had the Teamsters and nobody else. And the hon. member, whose interest in the Teamsters and the CLC are at
April 15, 1970

The Budget-Mr. Kievans least as great, I would have thought, as his interest in seeing that justice is done to the CNTU, became very quiet.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

I am simply telling the hon. member that. I am not the one who raised that conversation. He raised it, not me. He suggests that I committed a heinous offence in not including in my tenders the following three clauses: that whoever gets a tender must subscribe to and guarantee the job security of those who work for the firm that had lost the tender; that those who get a tender must guarantee the salaries, after they employ them, of those who worked for the firm that lost the tender; and that those who get a tender must agree to take in and certify the union of those who had lost the tender, regardless of what unions they may have had, what employees they may have had or what this might have done to their prevailing wage rates. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, why in hell should you ask for tenders if you are going to put in this type of condition; and who is going to submit quotations in response to tenders that contain such conditions?
I am as sensitive as the hon. member to the fact that labour legislation may swing this way some day, and perhaps it should swing this way some day; but I say to him that when it does, and if it does, it should be after a full-scale debate in this House in which all of us decide that that is what we want, and not in reply to bullets through windshields or violence in the streets of Montreal.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is not very much more I want to say about this matter, except that the government has been patient, it has been tolerant and it has been generous. It has used up several ministers in the process.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, I may say it. When those of us who have been involved in this began to lose a little patience, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)-and I applaud him for it-wisely decided that he would bring in my colleague, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury), whose patience is limitless and had not been used up. I must say that I, as Postmaster General, appreciate all that he has done in the past several weeks to achieve a solution. I applaud him and thank him for what he has done, not only for me personally

but also for the 48,000 people who work in the Post Office, for the rest of this government and particularly for the people of Canada.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to take a few minutes to entertain the House on a subject not connected with the Post Office, but which is extremely important for a great number of my fellow citizens, and also for a great number of Canadians from other constituencies.
I should like to illustrate that we must urgently take steps to protect a homegrown industry, namely the textile products industry.
In the past years, this law-abiding industry has behaved as a good citizen. We should therefore give it the consideration it deserves. It played an important part during the war, and thereby not only won the praise of the public, but is also entitled to its gratitude.
The textile industry is going through very difficult times. It is not looking for charity nor is it asking for subsidies, but it does want to know if the present government wants a Canadian textile industry or not. It wants to continue sharing in the development of Canada and providing employment for Canadians. Workers in the textile industry are not seeking favours, they merely want the opportunity to continue working at a trade they have been practicing for a long time in order to be able to provide for their families.
Labour unions are not asking for favours either, they only want to go on working to improve the conditions of workers in this industry and prevent them from becoming unemployed.
All these good citizens want only one thing, and they deserve it: more attention from the government.
Let us examine rapidly the official figures in order to find out what the textile and clothing industry means to Canada.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
The textile industry has been established in the province of Quebec since 1845. Indeed, the first textile plant or mill as we used to say was founded in the city of Sherbrooke.
Today, the textile industry has 37 plants and employs 83,000 Canadians. In the province of Quebec, 47,000 people earn their living in primary textile products industries. In Ontario and the Maritimes, many have found
April 15, 1970

a job in the textile industry. In Quebec, the annual production of primary textile products is valued at $850 million. From 1946 to 1967, the cotton industry spent the impressive amount of $350 million on the construction and repairs of buildings alone. From 1960 to 1964, the productivity of textile plants increased almost fivefold.
During the past ten years, it is interesting to note that the price of textile products has remained almost the same. There has been only a slight increase and this in spite of the fact that the industry had to face the problem of salary increases and higher costs for services and transport.
As for the clothing industry, it provides employment to 110,000 workers, 50,000 of them in Montreal, 19,000 in Toronto and 6,000 in Winnipeg.
Let me remind you that in the forties, the Canadian textile industry supplied about 75 per cent of the domestic market. Today, it scarcely supplies 60 per cent of the consumption and if the present economic conditions persist, it is to be expected, Mr. Speaker, that its share of the Canadian market will dwindle even more. What are the reasons for the smaller share of the Canadian market going to the Canadian industry? Imports from countries where labour is cheap are mainly responsible for that.
I would like at this stage to quote a few statistics to better enlighten the House on the conditions existing in this industry.
Imports from Japan, which were 2 million pounds in 1954, have now reached 37 million pounds. In 1954 imports from Asia totalled 4 million pounds, today they amount to 47 million pounds. In 1954, we were importing one million pounds of textile products from eastern Europe, when today 20 million pounds find their way into Canada. From low income countries we were importing half a million pounds in 1954, and today we get 15 million pounds from them.
As far as the United States are concerned, their exports to Canada have increased from 68 million pounds in 1954 to 110 million pounds today.
Our imports from the United Kingdom are still much the same, that is 26 million pounds annually.
These increases in our imports, Mr. Speaker, have resulted in 5,000 fewer jobs since 1966. As for the shirt industry, statistics are shocking.
The Budget-Mr. Ricard
One can read at page 36 of a publication entitled L'avenir du textile et du vetement au Quebec, the following:
Our industry makes up 50 per cent of the total market. In 1966, total imports of shirts represented only 25 per cent of the whole market. Imports have doubled in less than three years.
Further on, the following comparison is given:
In 1965, domestic production amounted to 1,841,000 dozens: imports, to roughly 750,000 dozens.
In 1966, domestic production amounted to 1,674,000 dozens; imports, to 764,000 dozens. In 1967, domestic production was 1,477,000 dozens and imports 1,042,000 dozens. In 1968, domestic production amounted to 1,296,000 dozens and imports to 1,400,000 dozens.
I go back to the quotation:
In the first three months of 1969, total imports of shirts increased by 70,000 dozens-
Such statistics are surely conducive to some concern on our part. They constitute warnings of which the government should take note even now.
The leaders of the textile and clothing industries, as well as those of labour unions have been expecting the government to come out with a textile policy, but it has yet to come.
A few statements have already been made on the matter.
The April 7 issue of the Globe & Mail gives an account of what was said by Mr. E. Douglas James, President of the Cotton Institute of Canada and of Cosmos Imperial Mills Limited, of Toronto, a company employing 1,500 workers. I quote:

If they say they don't want a textile industry we will be ready to close down our mills. If they say they want a viable industry we're prepared to stay.
When Mr. James says "they", he means the government.

In the same article, we can also find what was said by Mr. Gerald Bruck, President of Bruck Mills Limited, of Montreal. Here is what it says, and I quote:

The plants are in great shape. They (the manufacturers) are paying a lot for labour and they are pressured by imports.
Mr. B. S. Saunders, managing director of Wabasco in Montreal, says:
This lack of information is like going to the doctor and getting all the x-rays taken and having

April 15, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Ricard
him say, "come back in two weeks" and six months later still nothing has happened.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)

It would be interesting to know what the officials of some industries, one of which is a local one, are thinking. I have here a letter addressed to me by Mr. Midgley, Vice-President and General Manager of Penman's Limited, which reads in part as follows:

You undoubtedly know that the government is in the process of considering the above-mentioned subject and that an announcement is expected in the near future. For many years, the industry has called upon the government for a statement of policy. The main problem which has just been made public, and with which you are conversant, is that of "imports at low prices".
The need of a policy is proving obvious, because manufacturers want to determine whether their position is viable before making capital available in the future for investments which could create new jobs. Canadian manufacturers supply at the present time only 50 per cent of the domestic textile market. We are the only country with such a fully developed industry to tolerate imports of goods at low prices in such quantities that they become the cause of such harmful pressures.
What we are seeking is a statement of policy concerning the role which our industry will be called upon to play in Canada, in order to prepare adequate plans.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian textile industry wants to know whether or not this government wishes it to continue its operations. For 1967 alone, if the products which came from countries with low production costs had been manufactured in Canada, the Canadian textile industry could have offered 20,000 more jobs than it does now.
Is it the intention of the government to give the death blow to the textile industry? It is time that those interested in this industry know what the situation is, and that as soon as possible.
When we consider the efforts made by management in this industry and its longtime investments in Canada, it seems desirable to limit imports so that the Canadian industry may rely on 70 per cent of the Canadian market. As I say, the Canadian industry does not want subsidies; it only wants to know whether the government really wants it to carry on. It is a very simple and straightforward question. It is time for the government, who has been beating around

the bush for months, to stop doing so, in the best interests, not only of the industry but also of the workers and of their families to whom it provides their daily bread.
Is it really to much to ask the government to take the necessary steps in order to preserve one of our oldest industries? I do not think so.
I believe that it could be possible to allow this industry to provide more jobs, since, according to its own information, if it could be assured of a share representing 70 per cent of the Canadian market, it could, from now until 1975, guarantee 16,000 or 18,000 extra jobs.
Since the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) spends millions of dollars to promote new industries, it would probably be only logical to try, at least, to keep those already existing in this country. I believe that I am not asking too much and I wish the responsible minister, that is the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), would tell the public, and this, as soon as possible, what the government policy towards the textile industry will be in the years to come.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, although it is a little over a month since the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) presented his budget, I expected to receive more comments than I did as I travelled through my constituency during the Easter recess.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The people know it is no use commenting.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It may be that the budget was received by the people as a sort of anticlimax, the minister having received his due share of public attention during the past few months. This is not to say that the budget that he presented did not parallel his previous budget as to the timeliness and appropriate measures which it contained. We are all aware that inflation was the No. 1 problem around which he had to build his budget. I think the government is to be commended for the introduction of credit controls.
I recently raised a question in the House on the indiscriminatory manner in which leading financial institutions and various companies engaged in retailing are distributing credit cards. I am pleased to see that the government is investigating the use of credit cards and the effect these cards are having on inflation. It is my contention that this credit could serve Canada far better if it were granted in order to increase the productivity and efficiency of this country. It is through increased
April 15, 1970	COMMONS
productivity and efficiency that we will break the back of inflation, and not through the indiscriminate distribution of credit cards. I am thinking of the man, for example, who could be given the same credit with which to expand his plant, to buy more efficient machinery, to update his manufacturing methods to lower the cost of his products, thereby helping to beat inflation and also to create more jobs.
In the minister's reference to the economic prospects and fiscal outlook for the coming year he anticipates that the growth rate will be lower by between 1.5 per cent and 2 per cent than last year's rate of 4.8 per cent. Wlhile there will be an increase in employment, it will not keep pace with the growth of the labour force, resulting in an increase in unemployment. The latter is evident now. In this respect, in my opinion the record should be set straight. This government is not using unemployment as a tool to fight inflation, as implied by certain opposition members of this House and certain groups outside. No government, Mr. Speaker, could be so callous or cruel. I for one could not be party to such action.
To me, labour leaders today should show the same foresight as leaders in the business community did in co-operating with the Prices and Incomes Commission in trying to control price increases, instead of their present attitude of criticizing the government's attempt to fight inflation. We are all aware that every labour union in this country is an autonomous group. Nevertheless, the men who speak nationally for labour might well have endorsed in principle a policy of wage restraint during this critical period and in so doing displayed leadership to the men and groups they represent. Surely labour should be co-operating with the government and be thinking of the job security of their workers, because indeed, Mr. Speaker, if they do not inflation will continue and unemployment will increase in direct ratio to the rate of inflation.
Another matter I would like to bring to the attention of this House is a recent statement made by the Governor of the Bank of Canada, who stated that 7.75 million man-days were lost as a result of Canadian strikes in 1969. These strikes and the hardships they cause to the membership of the union, the business and the community involved are, in my opinion, another direct effect of inflation. Unless inflation is brought under control we can look for more strikes, more bitterness and more strain. So inflation is not only a dollars and cents proposition; it tears at the very
DEBATES	5915
The Budget-Mr. Whiting fabric of Canadian life by dividing us in this way. So again I call upon labour to co-operate with the Prices and Incomes Commission in its efforts to control rising prices. This cannot help but improve employment conditions.
It is no secret, Mr. Speaker, that I represent the riding with the highest per capita income in Canada. This means that my constituents are presently carrying a better than average taxation load. So it is no wonder that they are most concerned by the effects the final version of the white paper will have on their lives.
I was pleased when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in his speech at a fund-raising dinner in Toronto, reassured the people of Canada that the white paper contained proposals only and the legislation which will ultimately be brought before this House will contain many of the suggested changes submitted by thoughtful people. I was pleased because this was an assurance to the people of Halton who have taken the time to make many worth-while suggestions that we will end up with a tax structure that will be fair and equitable. Although I have received a few "nut" letters, the majority of the hundreds I have received have been constructive and well thought out.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
The great majority of these letters were primarily concerned with the deemed realization of capital gains every five years in equity ownership of widely held Canadian corporations and the elimination of the preferred tax rate on the first $35,000 of corporate earnings which would have its greatest effect on small companies. For example, the Oakville Chamber of Commerce in their letter to me stated that the deemed realization of shares in widely held Canadian corporations is discriminatory and elimination of the preferred tax would be punitive. However, I am happy to see that the Minister of Finance has already stated and has asked the committees studying the white paper to consider some method to offset the adverse effect that an increased tax would have on small companies.
I wish to make a suggestion to the members of the committees. I believe they should call in officials from the Industrial Development Bank when this proposal is being studied. I believe that the Industrial Development Bank could provide the committee with a lot of very useful information in this area, because they are dealing constantly with small businessmen and businessmen in general and they know their problems.
April 15, 1970

The Budget-Mr. Whiting
Other suggestions I received were concerned with the proposed capital gains tax on the appreciation in the value of homes and personal possessions. It was felt that it was unrealistic and should be changed. A $1,000 limit in Halton is not feasible because houses have appreciated $2,000 and more per year. I have the figures to prove this. I urge the committee to study this proposal very carefully because I hope it is not the government's intention to collect taxes on the sale of private homes. I hope it is not the intention to tax a man who, say, receives a promotion or wishes to upgrade his living standard and sells his old home at a capital gain in excess of $1,000 per year, plus the cost of repairs, to buy a more expensive home: Surely it is not the intention to penalize this individual. Many other letters dealt with the proposals to increase tax on earning from $10,000 to $20,000 per year.
If the legislation, when enacted, produces the surplus projected, I recommend to this House that this surplus be used to reduce the tax burden, rather than launching into any more universal welfare programs. I must say that most of my constituents are in favour of the principle of capital gains but do not agree that it be set at the same rate as that of income, and further, that should a capital gains tax become law, the estates tax should be substantially reduced or abolished.
I think that I have received a directive from my constituents through these letters and comments, and I believe this is the case with every member of this House. I therefore regard it as my duty as the member for Halton to express the views of my constituents and to represent these views in this House. The people of Halton have been genuine in their desire to play a part in participatory democracy. Many have written me more than once, clarifying and sometimes tempering their suggestions or strengthening the points they had made previously. I have met through their letters people in my riding whom I might never have been in contact with otherwise. It has been a warm experience in most cases, as have been the meetings I have attended. Courtesy by those who disagree has been impressive. I was pleased that my coupon mail showed that almost everyone knew their member's name. It was not because of my constituents that Mr. Brown lost his Ottawa post office.
I would now like to discuss a problem which is of vital concern to me and to many other members of this House. Over the past

two years I have been called upon by three municipalities in my riding-Acton, Georgetown and Milton-which have received what might almost be termed ultimatums from our national railways. Canadian National Railways advised the town of Acton that they proposed to remove the agent and all railway business would be transacted from their Guelph master agency. I dealt with this in my maiden speech. Apparently, the CNR did not get the copy of Hansard I sent them because the station agent was subsequently removed.
The town of Georgetown has received word that certain passenger trains which have served the people of Georgetown for many years are to be discontinued. A hearing was held before the Railway Transport Committee of the Canadian Transport Commission. This discontinuance of service will also affect the town of Acton. The town of Milton received word from Canadian Pacific Railway that it intended to curtail passenger train service in that community. Previously, four trains serviced Milton, but now this service has been cut in half. Canadian National Railways has long since discontinued passenger service here also.
It would appear that when either of the railways set upon a course of action there is little that can be done to stop them. It is true that hearings are held, but having attended and participated in the hearing held in Acton I am convinced it is little more than shadowboxing. The communities have really no facilities at their disposal, while the railways appear with their pseudo experts armed with their slide rules and brief case loaded with data and statistics, but not necessarily relevant facts. It all looks very sincere, honest and impressive, but it always seems there is one thing overlooked-the people. Of course, standing up for the people is like being in favour of motherhood in the eyes of the commissioners. Nevertheless, there is something lost in the community when railroads take these actions. A way of life that has helped to make these communities a desirable place to live is being taken away. And further, these changes create many inconveniences. For example, the discontinuance of the trains in Georgetown will have a far-reaching impact upon the public's convenience and necessity for transportation service, particularly between Georgetown and Toronto. These trains are used by people who wish to travel back and forth between the two communities as well as by regular commuters.
April 15, 1970	COMMONS
We hear a lot today that we should guard with all our might against impeding the development of small business, but what about the small communities? Should we not have equal regard for them? I think we should. It would seem that in any decisions that are handed down by the Transport Commission, the benefits that would accrue to the railroads are always upheld. Of course, the plea of the railroads at any of these hearings is the need for economy, but are the railroads the only -consideration in cases of this kind? I believe that decisions of this nature have broader implications and go far beyond the Canadian Transport Commission.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Our highways, for example, are being plugged with automobiles, and ways and means must be found to alleviate this situation. The cost of building highways is astronomical. Train service is one of the answers: this is proved by the Go train service running east and west out of Toronto. While highways are a matter of provincial jurisdiction, nevertheless this does not prevent the railways from co-operating with the provinces, with federal backing. The railways have played a dominant role in the building of Canada and they are responsible for the location of many of our present day communities. They have contributed to the prosperity of those communities. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker the railways have a new role to play. There is a growing transportation problem in this country and the railways must provide part of the solution. Highways cost money, and if the railways will lessen the need for highways, why should we demand that every branch line and every station has to pay its way? The federal government should have something to say. I believe it is time we had a national transportation policy.
