speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Welfare, Mr. Speaker, is a part of any budget. Any way which can be found *of reducing these charges means a reduction in taxes for all taxpayers. More than costs are involved. In my opinion, one of the greatest social injustices we have in Canada is that suffered by deserted wives and children. Not only does the husband who deserts throw the support of his family on the shoulders of the taxpayers, but he can run around Canada without responsibilities, having himself a fine old time. If he can be located, then our courts can take the necessary action to make him assume his share of the burden of raising his
DEBATES	5917
The Budget-Mr. Whiting family and housing his wife. But I was surprised to find out how hard this location problem is for the wives.
Remember, these are women who are suddenly left alone, without means of support other than mothers' allowance paid by the province, of which the federal government pays half, and any welfare assistance they are able to secure. Her state of existence is surely one to wrench at your heartstrings. I recommend that hon. members who are not lawyers should take the time to talk to family court judges in their ridings and listen to them outlining the problems they face in trying to assist these deserted wives. I have had discussions with the provincial family court judge, Judge Kenneth Langdon, in my riding of Hal ton. I have also discussed this question with lawyers, social workers and police officials. They all agree that this is a pressing and serious problem.
Let me give the House an example of one case which occurred in my own constituency. A mother with four children, two of them of pre-school age, called me requesting some assistance in obtaining a Canada Manpower retraining course. Her husband would not give her any money to buy food for herself and her children; they were two months behind with the rent and other obligations; any day she expected to find the bailiff at her door. In order to put food on the table and clothe herself and the children she did housework, taking the two younger children with her. Her husband had found other interests which took most of his time and most of his money. A clerk-typist course was not the answer.
A court order was issued and the husband was made to pay a portion of his earnings to his wife in order that she might provide for herself and her children. This woman, in my opinion, was one of the more fortunate wives inasmuch as the family court knew where the husband could be found and where he was employed. What would have happened to this family had this man run off, say, somewhere out west? In this case, as in so many others, the wife had no money to enable her to trace her husband. He gets off scot-free except for the tax he pays on his earnings; the taxpayers would have had to support his deserted family.
Now just suppose there were some way to trace these types of men. No one would want to force them to return to their wives, even if the wives would have them. But the courts can and would make them bear their financial
April 15, 1970

The Budget-Mr. Whiting responsibilities. The results would be that welfare costs in all parts of Canada would drop. Indeed, they would be dramatically reduced, since the number of deserted families is much higher than is generally realized.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
There would also be another advantage, not monetary but of real importance. The deserted family would no longer be on the welfare rolls. The sense of dignity for these women and children would be restored. They would be able to pay their way and hold their heads as high as they are entitled to do. For this reason I do not see this primarily as a taxation problem, although it is an expensive one. It is a "just society" action to find some way to locate these deserters effectively, economically and quickly.
Before I outline a possible solution to this problem of how to trace these husbands I want to emphasize two main points. First, in Ontario when fathers are separated from or leave their children, at the time funds are to be made available from provincial or local welfare agencies to buy food, clothing and to care for them they insist that a charge be laid against the husband under the Deserted Wives and Children Maintenance Act.
Second, where there are children under 16 separated from their fathers for whatever reason, the provincial judge in all cases makes an order ordering the father to support these children. Regardless of why a husband or father is living apart from the children, he is legally obliged to provide support. I should like to add that it is of deep concern to me that the obligation is only valid until the child reaches age 16. I believe that serious consideration should be given to raising this age limit.
In my opinion, when a provincial judge hands down an order that a deserting father or a deserting husband must make payment to his family for their support, and his whereabouts are not known, the judge should be able to request the most up-to-date information as to where the husband or father might be found. Here, Mr. Speaker, is where I believe the federal government could be of substantial assistance to the provinces. When a provincial family court judge would like to know the whereabouts of a husband or a father, he could notify an appropriate provincial department; for example, in Ontario it could be the Department of Social and Family Service. This department in turn could contact the federal government requesting the TMr. Whiting.]
last known address of this husband and father in question. How much information is now available at the federal level is not known to me. However, I believe a pool of such information could be obtained from the Unemployment Insurance Commission, the Canada Pension Plan and other branches of government which might be used to provide this source of information.
If we put the two things together, the evasion of responsibility by individuals so that others have to pay and the reduction of the number of families on welfare, surely it would be in the interest of all Canadians, except those husbands who want to "live the life of Riley", if we were to examine this problem in depth. This is another area where the federal government could show leadership. I am sure this would receive the co-operation of all the provinces, the provincial family courts, welfare workers and every municipality, because they realize the seriousness of this problem. I would suggest, therefore, that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) include a recommendation to this effect in the white paper on social welfare which he proposes to present to this House in the near future; or perhaps this could be made the subject of separate action on his part.
I believe that some method of tracing these men could be found that would be practical, economical and which would not run counter to our Canadian way of life or our civil liberties. If we can liberalize, as we have done, the laws on abortion for the betterment of women, we must also be able to find a way to make a family court a place where something can be done for those women who so desperately look to the law to right their wrongs, instead of the way it is at present.

speakeroldname: Mr. Walter C. Carter (St. John's West):
maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was interested in some of the remarks made by the preceding speaker, the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Whiting). I was particularly interested in what he had to say about the suggestion that has been made from this side of the House that this government is deliberately setting about to create unemployment. I am not sure that I got the hon. member's words correctly, but I believe he said he would not want to be part of a government that would deliberately set about to create unemployment.
Let me remind the hon. member that his leader, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), has said on television that if necessary he and the
April 15, 1970

government which he heads is prepared to drive the unemployment figure to 6 per cent to curb inflation. In light of that statement and the remarks made by the hon. member, I wonder whether he would want to be a part of this government which would drive the unemployment figure to 6 per cent or more. I am sure, after what he has said this afternoon, that he would not want to support the Prime Minister and this government which would set out to achieve this aim, that is, to deliberately create unemployment to the point where it reached a national average of over 6 per cent.
I look at this budget as a Member of Parliament concerned-

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am more concerned with what has happened in the past year and how the unemployment figure has been driven up because of this government's phony war on inflation. I can understand the hon. member's lack of concern for unemployment because, by his own admission a moment ago, he said he represents a riding that has the highest per capita income in Canada. I am not surprised to know that he is not too concerned with what is happening on the national scene with regard to unemployment.
Nor is the hon. member concerned about the deliberate attempt on the part of the government he supports to drive unemployment to the point where it has become almost unbearable to a large segment of our population, especially those 500,000 Canadians who have been forced to go on the rolls of the unemployed. This is the result of the heartless and cruel policies of the government which he supports, which has deliberately driven the unemployment figure to the point it has now reached.
I look at this budget as a Member of Parliament concerned with Canada as a whole and as a Member of Parliament with particular
The Budget-Mr. Carter interest in and a duty to the constituency of St. John's West. From whatever point I view it, it is something like a cat that was dragged in. As I said before, we have a government which has deliberately set out to create unemployment. As if it is not enough that it should set out deliberately to force men out of jobs and onto the unemployment rolls, this government has the brazen gall to brag about it. We have heard the Prime Minister say that if necessary he is prepared to see the unemployment figure go to 6 per cent. We have heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) make similar remarks. As I said before, not only is the government taking this stand and adopting this policy with that effect, but it has the gall to brag about it.
It is perfectly obvious to most of us, and indeed to most Canadians, that the economic policies of this government as represented by the Budget at this stage guarantees no assurance of success and no assurance that it can beat inflation without ruinous results. It is also perfectly clear from the Budget address that inflation is not being licked. We have no better evidence of that than the evidence given by the Minister of Finance. He forecast a reduction in the real growth of the gross national product of 3 per cent this year. The major consequence of this lower growth rate is an unemployment level ranging over the year at 6 per cent.
During the past two years much has been made of the fact that this government was elected on the charisma of the Prime Minister who made no promise except to build a just society. It is quite obvious to this House and to the majority of Canadians that the Prime Minister did not keep that promise. In fact, he has done just the opposite; he has built an unjust society. Obviously the government is anxious to keep the Prime Minister's Christmas promise of a 6 per cent unemployment figure. This, of course, means much higher levels in the low-growth areas and in areas which are subject to seasonal employment fluctuations.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
In this country and during this decade a federal government budget is of immense importance. By experience and common sense, and because of a desire to do great and noble things, the people of this country have given our government vast fiscal and monetary powers. The government does not have these powers for petty reasons. Generous and talented people have charged the

April 15. 1970
The Budget-Mr. Carter government with the task of leading us in shaping a fulfilled society. Essentially, the policy of Canada is the pursuit of common goals to end uncertainty, to end poverty, to moderate the causes of strife, to help Canada grow, to improve and make things work, and to keep the country and make it ours.
In diverse expression these common goals are being sought by 21 million people. My colleagues and I consider it our right and responsibility to judge the present government's budget in terms of these energetic, national goals. It is from this standpoint that we condemn this budget of the Liberal government. Frankly, we hold the opinion and the suspicion that good government in Canada is somewhere in exile.
In terms of historic experience, the reduced growth of our gross national product and higher unemployment should have a substantial dampening effect on inflationary tendencies, but in Canada today we have a different situation. Prices and wages still continue to increase to what the Minister of Finance calls unacceptable levels. The meaning, of course, is unmistakable. Despite a downturn in the economy and higher unemployment, the inflationary forces at work in the economy are not yielding. The minister admits in his statement that it is particularly hazardous to try to make any forecast of price and income changes in the balance of this year.
This inflation has not disappeared as it should have. The government's restrictive fiscal and monetary policies have not budged it. Prices keep on rising. The interesting question we must ask ourselves-I am sure most Canadians are asking it-is what the situation will be six months from now, with unemployment running at deliberately increased levels in order to produce a slack in demand while inflation is still continuing at or near the present level.
The minister is confronted with a dilemma for which so far he has no answer except to pray that the Prices and Incomes Commission will have an impact on the economy. So far the results do not appear to indicate that is likely to be forthcoming. The Prices and Incomes Commission, as laudable an effort as it may be, has not at all shown that it can achieve price stability in the economy. It has no teeth and no power to force labour to enlist in the anti-inflation fight. In fact, the budget speech notes that there will be difficult wage negotiations this year with perhaps several costly, prolonged strikes. This, again, is an

outright admission by the minister that costs, and consequently prices, will continue to escalate in 1970.
In a return tabled in this House some time ago it was very interesting to note that the co-chairmen of the Prices and Incomes Commission are being paid $40,000 a year. As the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) would say, they have won then-war on poverty. I think the half million people out of work in this country, many of them forced to be jobless by a cruel and heartless government which deliberately creates unemployment, will be heartened to know the men working for them to keep prices down and spike the inflationary psychology are doing very well at $40,000 a year.
It is quite obvious that as a result of the present policies of this government unemployment will continue to be very high. Inflation apparently will continue. Will the answer simply be even more tightening of the screw? How much unemployment is socially or politically acceptable in the name of beating inflation? The Minister of Finance, on CTV's Question Period show, said that higher unemployment may be necessary if we are really to beat inflation. This is a shocking statement. I would refer also to the remarks of the hon. member for Halton who a moment ago expressed the opinion that he would not want to be a part of any government that would deliberately set about to create unemployment.
The record will show that the Minister of Finance on this CTV program did admit that it may be necessary to increase unemployment in order to beat inflation. I think there is in Canada a great deal of sympathy for the Minister of Finance. I believe he has shown some real determination to beat inflation. I am sure he has taken some very serious political risk. So far, however, his policy has not done the job. The minister's speech implies that if it does not work in the next six months, at the moment he does not have any better ideas. It is quite obvious that the minister and his leader, the Prime Minister, and indeed the government as a whole are gambling on a theory that may or may not work. I think this is a very serious matter, because in so doing he is inflicting a lot of suffering, perhaps unnecessary suffering, on the Canadian public, on the taxpayers and on our working force. I feel this is a very serious and dangerous course on which the government has embarked.
April 15, 1970

For the sake of Canada and our unemployed I hope this policy will work, but like my colleagues and most other Canadians I have very grave doubt whether the government's anti-inflationary policy will prove to be in the best interests of Canada and will indeed work as it has planned. It would appear to be pretty obvious that there will be another budget this fall. The indicators at this point suggest that even sterner measures will be taken. The minister's measures have not worked to date. They are not likely to work any better in the next six months. The minister will be back here in the House with another budget. He will be pouring on more restraints and taxes. I believe the unemployment figure must not be allowed to increase even further in order to help the minister prove his point that the policies he has adopted and those of his colleagues in the cabinet will have the desired effect of beating the inflation which we have in Canada at this time.
I should like to make a few remarks about the consumer credit controls proposed by the minister. How effective will these controls really be? The 20 per cent down payment and the 24 months' period for repayment are not very far from normal practice. Even the minister's own advisers are sceptical of his estimate that the effect will be to reduce consumer spending by about $400 million. The people in the credit business estimate the figure to be only about half that. What is $400 million, anyway? If that figure is accurate, consumer spending in Canada in 1970 will be about $49 billion instead of $49.4 billion.
The potential loopholes in the program envisaged by the minister are innumerable. The minister says he does not expect any buying spree in the next few weeks before the controls are imposed. I am sure we can all visualize dealers in some of the remote parts of Canada who are saddled with large surplus stocks offering in the next few weeks no down payment and seven years to pay if for no reason other than to move their stock.
These controls on credit will hurt the people who contribute least to inflation. The Prime Minister told reporters outside the House last week that this measure would protect the little guy. I say that is hogwash. It will not protect the little guy; it will make things much tougher for him in trying to obtain employment to earn enough to keep body and soul together and to retain his independence.
The Budget-Mr. Carter
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
As I have said, the program appears to be full of loopholes. In fact, the government appears not to have thought about the details of the program at all. There are dozens of ways in which the program could be circumvented, and the government has not really built up much legal justification for the controls, which might prevent a constitutional challenge from the provinces.
So we have a government that has quite obviously embarked on a policy of which they are not too sure. They are not convinced in their own minds that the policy to curb inflation on which they have embarked will work. They are gambling with the lives and the livelihood of the Canadian people, the average working man in Canada. By their own admission they have set about to deliberately create unemployment, hoping that this will have the desired effect of curbing inflation. I am convinced, and I am sure that many Canadians will agree with me, that they are wrong.
Their policy, which has been pretty well adopted right across the board, according to which the "have not" provinces are being forced to take the same medicine as the "have" provinces, where the people in the economically depressed areas of Canada are being forced to take the same medicine as that dished out to the better off provinces, is wrong too.
I should inform the minister that in my province of Newfoundland there is no sign of inflation. Inflation down there is pretty well a foreign word. Unemployment is probably at its highest peak since Confederation. At present it is estimated to be approaching the 22 per cent mark. The national unemployment figure rose to 6.5 per cent, while in the Atlantic region it is 11 per cent or 12 per cent. There are provinces, such as the one which I have the honour to represent where the unemployment figure is reported to approach the 22 per cent level. This has been brought about largely by the government's illogical policy with regard to inflation and its attempts to curb inflation.
I am convinced, and I am sure other members will agree, that while we have inflation in certain areas of Canada, we should not penalize people in the depressed areas, which is what is happening. I think the Premier of Nova Scotia was right when he said that the present government's policy can be likened to a family in which one child is sick but the entire family is being forced to take the same
The Budget-Mr. Carter medicine. In Canada there are certain areas where inflation is present, but we should not impose the same restrictions and policies on the "have not" or economically depressed areas where inflation is a foreign word.
This government must accept its responsibilities to all the regions of Canada and must make good its promise to bring an end to regional disparity. In the past couple of years we have heard much talk about the Prime Minister's so-called just society. We have heard much talk about bringing an end to regional disparity. But so far we have seen very little action. I grant that certain measures are being taken by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion to help some of the "have not" areas in Canada, including the Atlantic region; but I am not convinced that these measures will be sufficient to bring about an end to disparity and to bring the "have not" areas of Canada up to a level where they can enjoy the status of first-class citizens.
In Canada a large number of people do not enjoy the status of first-class citizens. I can think of a large segment of our population in Newfoundland which does not enjoy the rights and the status of first-class Canadians. Until such time as Canada can give all its people equal rights and equal opportunities. I do not think we can boast of the influence that we have in certain parts of the nation and say that all our citizens are being treated alike and enjoy the status of first-class citizens.
April 15, 1970
Many measures have been taken by the government in recent months that have had a detrimental effect on the provinces. We have seen the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans) close down a large number of post offices. The argument that he is using is that it is cheaper to initiate the rural delivery system than to maintain the present post offices in various parts of Canada, especially in my riding of St. John's West. I think the Postmaster General's policies are wrong. I think time will prove that the system he is now trying to inaugurate will eventually cost more than it would have cost to retain our present post offices and the system under which a large number of the smaller outports in Newfoundland, and indeed in the west of Canada operate.
I would liken the Postmaster General to someone who is groping in the dark and who is trying to find an answer to some of the problems that are obviously facing his department. I do not think that the elimination of post offices in Canada-and I can speak with some authority for my riding-is the answer, and time will prove that the Postmaster General is wrong.
In the matter of the fishery, which of course is very important in the Atlantic areas of Canada, we have serious problems.

subtopic: U.S. PRESS RELEASE ON CANADA'S CLAIM TO JURISDICTION OVER ARCTIC POLLUTION AND TERRITORIAL SEA LIMITS

speechtext:

Following is text of statement to be released by State dept at noon briefing Apr 15. Text begins.
Last week the Cdn govt introduced in the House of Commons two bills dealing with pollution in the arctic, fisheries and the limits of the territorial sea. The enactment and implementation of these measures would affect the exercise by the USA and other countries of the right to freedom of the seas in large areas of the high seas and would adversely affect our efforts to reach innatl agreement on the use of the seas.
The bills seek to establish pollution zones in arctic waters up to 100 miles from every point of cdn coastal territory above the 60th parallel. Within these zones, cda would assert the right to control all shipping, to prescribe standards of vessel construction, navigation and operation, and to prohibit, if CDA deemed it necessary, the free passage of vessels in those waters. Additionally, the legislation seeks to authorize the establishment of exclusive CDN fisheries in areas of the high seas beyond 12 miles, such as the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the Bay of Fundy, and of a 12-mile territorial sea off CDAs coasts.
Innatl law provides no/no basis for these proposed unilateral extensions of jurisdictions on the high seas, and the USA can neither accept nor acquiesce in the assertion of such jurisdiction.
We are concerned that this action by CDA if not/not opposed by us, would be taken as precedent in other parts of the world for other unilateral infringements of the freedom of the seas. If CDA had the right to claim and exercise exclusive pollution and resources jurisdiction on the high seas, other countries could assert the right to exercise jurisdiction for other purposes, some reasonable and some not/not, but all equally invalid according to innatl law, merchant shipping would be severely restr, and naval mobility would be seriously jeopardized. The potential for serious innatl dispute and conflict is obvious.
The USA has long sought innatl solutions rather than natl approaches to problems involving the high seas. We are working for appropriate action within the UN framework looking toward the conclusion of a new innatl treaty dealing with the limit of the territorial sea, freedom of transit through and over innatl straits and defining preferential fishing rights for coastal states on the high seas.
We are also seeking new innatl means for controlling pollution on the high seas. Last fall 47 countries, including the USA and CDA, participated in the preparation of two innatl conventions establishing the right of a coastal state to take certain ltd anti-pollution measures against vessels on the high seas, and also imposing strict liability upon the owners of vessels responsible for pollution. These conventions which the USA has recently signed were concluded under UN auspices at BRU. Other innatl approaches to control of pollution are underway at NATO and the UN. Moreover, the USA is acutely aware of the peculiar ecological nature of the arctic region, and the potential dangers of oil pollution in that area. The arctic is a region important to all nations in its unique environment, its increasing significance as a world trade route and as a source of natural resources.
